steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on MuLTI, an efficient video-and-language understanding framework with a Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler and a new Multiple Choice Modeling pretraining task. Lay out the two challenges it addresses (efficient feature fusion for long sequences, and the gap between pretraining and downstream tasks), how we tackle each, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Video-and-language understanding and its two open challenges
2. Challenge 1: feature fusion efficiency vs. accuracy
3. Challenge 2: domain gap between pretraining and downstream tasks
4. Our approach: Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler (and Figure 1 comparison)
5. Our approach: Multiple Choice Modeling (MCM)
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Intro
- applications: videoQA, text-video retrieval, multi-label classification
- significant progress, but two challenges: efficiency vs. performance on long sequences; domain gap pretraining vs. downstream
- model = text encoder + video encoder + feature fusion module; latter two -> high computational cost

2. Feature fusion
- concatenate video-text encoder outputs, transformer encoder -> complexity grows with sequence length squared
- condense video features (mean pooling / class tokens) before fusion -> risk losing critical details
- Flamingo: samplers + random queries for condensation; suboptimal, may compromise feature integrity
- balancing cost and accuracy still challenging
- following prior work: selectively freeze encoder components to lower visual encoder training cost

3. Pretraining / downstream gap
- four typical pretraining tasks: Masked Frame Modeling (MVM) for video encoder, MLM for text encoder, VTM and VTC for joint optimization
- effective for representations, but domain gaps remain, esp. videoQA
- only VTC consistent with text-video retrieval

4. Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler
- MuLTI: sampler for sequence condensation and multi-modal fusion
- existing: learnable query vector samples video feature via self-attention; random init query can discard vital info -> performance drop
- lightweight Adapt-Pooling: condensed features from importance of each sequence block
- add condensed features to sampled features; short text features sample and fuse long video features
- shared self-attention, separate feed forward networks per modality
- Figure 1: (a),(b) lengthy concatenated fusion -> lots of video memory; (b),(c) compress video features (longer than text), excessive compression hurts; (d) ours: condense text features for fusion, concise text directs video feature sampling -> better performance

5. MCM
- large-scale video-text pretraining helps significantly, but task gap remains for videoQA
- difficulty: constructing suitable question-answer pairs
- MCM: multiple-choice QA tasks built on large-scale video-text datasets
- find text description best matching the video from a randomly constructed collection -> better encoders and video-text alignment

6. Contributions
- (1) MuLTI: accurate, memory-efficient; feature sampling + attention modules
- (2) Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler: sample long sequences, video-text interaction, less memory, better performance
- (3) MCM; experiments on seven English tasks and one Chinese multi-label classification task
- designed for industrial long sequences, still handles short sequences well, state-of-the-art

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Video-and-language understanding has a lot of applications, such as video question answering (videoQA), text-video retrieval and multi-label classification. Existing methods have made significant progress on it. But they still have two challenges: balancing computational efficiency and performance when the sequences are long, and the domain gap between pretraining and downstream tasks.

A video-text model usually has three modules: a text encoder, a video encoder, and a feature fusion module. The last two usually cause high computational costs.

Feature fusion modules have challenges in both efficiency and effectiveness. Some previous studies concatenate the outputs of the video and text encoders and process them with transformer encoders, so the complexity grows with the square of the sequence length. Other studies reduce the computation by condensing video features with mean pooling or class tokens before the feature fusion, but this risks losing critical details. Flamingo uses samplers and random queries to condense the video features efficiently, but this approach is suboptimal and may compromise the feature integrity. So balancing the computational cost and the accuracy of the model in the feature fusion module is still challenging. Following prior work, we also look at selectively freezing parts of the encoders to lower the training cost of the visual encoder.

Aligning pretraining with downstream tasks is also challenging. Previous pretraining frameworks usually use four typical pretraining tasks: Masked Frame Modeling (MVM) tasks to optimize the video encoder, Masked Language Modeling (MLM) tasks to optimize the text encoder, and Video Text Matching (VTM) and Video Text Comparison (VTC) tasks to optimize the video and text encoders jointly. These methods have been shown to be effective for learning video and text representations, but there are still significant domain gaps between pretraining and downstream tasks, especially for videoQA. Among these pretraining tasks, only VTC is consistent with text-video retrieval. So narrowing the domain gap between pretraining and downstream tasks is still challenging.

- MuLTI: Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler for sequence condensation and multi-modal fusion
- existing: learnable query vector samples video feature via self-attention; random init can discard vital info -> performance drops
- lightweight Adapt-Pooling: condensed features via importance of each sequence block; add to sampled features; short text features sample/fuse long video features
- shared self-attention, separate feed forward networks per modality
- Figure 1: (a),(b) concatenated fusion -> much video memory; (b),(c) compress video, excessive compression hurts; (d) ours, concise text guides video sampling -> better performance
- MCM: pretraining helps but task gap for videoQA; hard part = suitable QA pairs; multiple-choice QA on large video-text datasets; pick text matching video from random collection -> better encoders and alignment
- contributions (1) MuLTI (2) sampler (3) MCM; seven English tasks + one Chinese multi-label classification task
- built for industrial long sequences, also good on short ones, state-of-the-art

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Video-and-language understanding has a lot of applications, such as video question answering (videoQA), text-video retrieval and multi-label classification. Existing methods have made significant progress on it. But they still have two challenges: balancing computational efficiency and performance when the sequences are long, and the domain gap between pretraining and downstream tasks.

A video-text model usually has three modules: a text encoder, a video encoder, and a feature fusion module. The last two usually cause high computational costs.

Feature fusion modules have challenges in both efficiency and effectiveness. Some previous studies concatenate the outputs of the video and text encoders and process them with transformer encoders, so the complexity grows with the square of the sequence length. Other studies reduce the computation by condensing video features with mean pooling or class tokens before the feature fusion, but this risks losing critical details. Flamingo uses samplers and random queries to condense the video features efficiently, but this approach is suboptimal and may compromise the feature integrity. So balancing the computational cost and the accuracy of the model in the feature fusion module is still challenging. Following prior work, we also look at selectively freezing parts of the encoders to lower the training cost of the visual encoder.

Aligning pretraining with downstream tasks is also challenging. Previous pretraining frameworks usually use four typical pretraining tasks: Masked Frame Modeling (MVM) tasks to optimize the video encoder, Masked Language Modeling (MLM) tasks to optimize the text encoder, and Video Text Matching (VTM) and Video Text Comparison (VTC) tasks to optimize the video and text encoders jointly. These methods have been shown to be effective for learning video and text representations, but there are still significant domain gaps between pretraining and downstream tasks, especially for videoQA. Among these pretraining tasks, only VTC is consistent with text-video retrieval. So narrowing the domain gap between pretraining and downstream tasks is still challenging.

To address these challenges, we introduce MuLTI, which has a Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler for sequence condensation and multi-modal fusion. Existing methods usually use a learnable query vector to sample the video feature through self-attention modules. But a randomly initialized query vector can throw away vital information from the original features, which causes performance drops. We design a lightweight Adapt-Pooling method in the Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler, which gets the condensed features by calculating how important each sequence block is. Then we add the condensed features to the sampled features, and we use the short text features to sample and fuse the long video features. In the sampler, the self-attention is shared and different feed forward networks are kept for different modalities.

Figure 1 shows that previous models (a) and (b) use a lot of video memory because of their lengthy concatenated feature fusion. Both (b) and (c) compress the video features, which is a common choice since video features are longer than text. But too much compression can hurt performance, because video features have rich information. We instead design MuLTI like (d), with the Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler to condense text features efficiently for fusion. Because text is more concise, we use the streamlined text to direct the sampling of video features, and this gives better performance.

Pretraining on large-scale video-text datasets can improve the performance of video-text models significantly. But there are still domain gaps between the existing pretraining tasks and the downstream tasks, specifically for videoQA. What makes it hard to bring videoQA into pretraining is constructing suitable question-answer pairs. To reduce the domain gap between pretraining and the downstream task for videoQA, we introduce a new pretraining task called Multiple Choice Modeling (MCM). MCM can bridge the task gap between pretraining and downstream tasks by building multiple-choice question answering tasks on large-scale video-text datasets. The model has to find the text description that best matches the video from a randomly constructed collection, and this improves the representation ability of the video and text encoders and the alignment between video and text features.

Our contributions are as follows:

(1) We propose MuLTI, a highly accurate and memory-efficient video-and-language framework, which does efficient and effective feature fusion with feature sampling and attention modules.

(2) We propose a Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler that samples long sequence features and helps the interactions between video and text features, which reduces memory cost and improves performance.

(3) We design a new pretraining task, Multiple Choice Modeling (MCM), to bridge the task gap between pretraining and downstream tasks. Experiments on seven English tasks and one Chinese multi-label classification task show that MuLTI is effective.

We designed MuLTI for industrial scenarios with long sequences, but it still handles short sequences well and gets state-of-the-art performance.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Video-and-language understanding has a wide range of applications such as video question answering (videoQA), text-video retrieval and multi-label classification [1]. Existing methods have made significant progress in video-and-language understanding. However, they still suffer from two challenges: balancing computational efficiency and performance when dealing with long sequences, and the domain gap between pretraining and downstream tasks.

A video-text model generally consists of three modules: a text encoder, a video encoder, and a feature fusion module. The latter two usually cause high computational costs.

Feature fusion modules face both efficiency and effectiveness challenges. Previous studies [2,3] concatenate video-text encoder outputs for processing by transformer encoders, with complexity growing with the square of the sequence length. Other studies [4,5,6,7] reduce computation by condensing video features via mean pooling or class tokens before feature fusion, risking the loss of critical details. Flamingo [8] employs samplers and random queries for efficient video feature condensation, though this approach is suboptimal and may compromise feature integrity. In summary, balancing computational cost and model accuracy in the feature fusion module remains challenging. Following [9,10,11,12,13], we explore strategies for selectively freezing encoder components to lower visual encoder training costs.

Aligning pretraining with downstream tasks is also challenging. Previous pretraining frameworks generally apply four typical pretraining tasks: Masked Frame Modeling (MVM) tasks [7,14,2,3] for video encoder optimization, Masked Language Modeling (MLM) tasks [15,10,12,16,11,4] for text encoder optimization, and Video Text Matching (VTM) and Video Text Comparison (VTC) tasks [11,16,2,5] for joint optimization of video and text encoders. Although these methods have proven effective in learning video and text representations, significant domain gaps remain between pretraining and downstream tasks, especially in videoQA. Among the above pretraining tasks, only VTC is consistent with text-video retrieval. In summary, narrowing the domain gap between pretraining and downstream tasks is still challenging.

To address these challenges, we introduce MuLTI, featuring a Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler for sequence condensation and multi-modal fusion. Existing methods typically use a learnable query vector to sample the video feature through self-attention modules [8]. However, a randomly initialized query vector can discard vital original feature information, causing performance drops. We design a lightweight Adapt-Pooling method in the Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler that obtains the condensed features by calculating the importance of each sequence block. We then add the condensed features to the sampled features and use short text features to sample and fuse long video features. In the sampler, we share the self-attention and keep different feed forward networks for different modalities.

Figure 1 shows that previous models (a) [2,3] and (b) [5] consume substantial video memory due to their lengthy concatenated feature fusion. Both (b) and (c) [8] compress video features, a common choice since video features are longer than text. However, excessive compression can impair performance because of the rich information in video features. In contrast, we design MuLTI like (d) and introduce the Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler to efficiently condense text features for fusion. Since text is more concise, we use the streamlined text to direct video feature sampling, which enhances performance.

Pretraining on large-scale video-text datasets can significantly improve the performance of video-text models. However, domain gaps remain between existing pretraining tasks and downstream tasks, specifically in videoQA. The difficulty of introducing videoQA into pretraining lies in constructing suitable question-answer pairs. To reduce the domain gap between pretraining and the downstream task in videoQA, we introduce a new pretraining task named Multiple Choice Modeling (MCM). MCM bridges the task gap between pretraining and downstream tasks by constructing multiple-choice question answering tasks on large-scale video-text datasets. It asks the model to find the text description that best matches the video from a randomly constructed collection, which enhances the representation ability of the video and text encoders and the alignment between video and text features.

The contributions can be summarized as follows:

(1) We propose MuLTI, a highly accurate and memory-efficient video-and-language framework that achieves efficient and effective feature fusion through feature sampling and attention modules.

(2) We propose a Text-Guided MultiWay-Sampler to sample long sequence features and facilitate interactions between video and text features, reducing memory cost and improving performance.

(3) We design a new pretraining task called Multiple Choice Modeling (MCM) to bridge the task gap between pretraining and downstream tasks. Experimental results on seven English tasks and one Chinese multi-label classification task demonstrate the effectiveness of MuLTI.

Although we designed MuLTI for industrial scenarios with long sequences, it still handles short sequences well and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
